title: The Soweto Plot Richard Maponya Held for Nearly Thirty Years
dek: In September 2007 a mall opened in Soweto on land Richard Maponya had bought in the late 1970s and refused to give up under apartheid.

story.event: Opening Maponya Mall in Soweto in 2007 on land he had held since the late 1970s
story.summary: Richard Maponya bought land in Soweto in the late 1970s intending to build a modern shopping centre, resisted apartheid-era attempts to take it and failed for years to develop it. In partnership with Zenprop and later Investec, he opened the 65,000 square metre Maponya Mall in Pimville, Soweto, on 27 September 2007; Nelson Mandela opened it. In July 2021, after his death, local residents protected it from looting.
paragraphs: On Thursday 27 September 2007, Nelson Mandela opened a shopping mall on Old Potchefstroom Road in Pimville, Soweto, across the road from a barber working out of a wooden shack. Its developer, Richard Maponya, had bought the land nearly thirty years before, meaning to build exactly this. "I was convinced the people really needed a (shopping) mall, I never stopped," he said as it opened.

Maponya had built his businesses inside apartheid's rules. Refused a licence for a clothing shop in the 1950s, he took a licence to sell food instead and grew a dairy that delivered milk by bicycle, then shops, a butchery, filling stations and car dealerships. Black traders, he recalled, "were always reminded that we were temporary sojourners in the cities." According to Fin24's report of the opening, he resisted several attempts by the apartheid government to take the Soweto land; his own plans to develop it, once even as a casino, came to nothing.

After apartheid ended, he found a partner. By 2005 he had a 50-50 deal with the developer Zenprop and was clear about the standard: "We will not compromise on quality. It will look like any other modern mall anywhere else." His reasoning was about the people around him. Soweto, he said, had some five million residents and no mall, so anyone wanting clothes, furniture or appliances had to travel into town. Some believed black shoppers preferred to spend their money elsewhere. He meant to prove otherwise.

Due in October 2006, the mall came nearly a year late and larger than first planned, at 65,000 square metres. Fin24 put the cost at R650 million, with Maponya and Zenprop holding 42.5% each and the bank Investec 15%. About 200 shops opened, employing more than 1,800 people, and Zenprop counted 100,000 visitors on the first day.

Maponya died in January 2020. In July 2021, when looting destroyed about a dozen malls and shops in Soweto, residents of Pimville formed a human chain around the gates of his mall. It was the only large mall in Soweto to survive.

quote.text: They are not like the weakling flower whose stem-hold is so light that it drops away before attaining fruition.  They hold on to life with all their might and say, "never will we let go till the fruit is ripe."
quote.source_title: Sadhana: The Realisation of Life, Project Gutenberg eBook #6842
quote.connection: Tagore describes people who hold on until the fruit is ripe, not out of grim duty but out of joy in the work. Maponya's decades with an empty plot could be read as endurance alone. His own words before the opening, that the mall excited him more than anything else he had done, sound closer to Tagore.

reflection: Most of Maponya's thirty years with that land were not spent building on it. They were spent running other businesses, waiting for laws to change, and declining to let one plot go. The long wait did not stop him working at everything else.

Some of what you hope to build may take longer than you would like, for reasons that are not yours to fix. Holding on is not the same as pushing every day. Tagore's point is that it can be done gladly, and gladness needs rest as much as it needs effort.
invitation: Name one long aim you cannot finish this year. Write down one part of the work towards it that you still enjoy, and do a little of that today without pushing for more.

sources.title: Maponya: a vote of confidence (27 September 2007)
sources.supports: The mall opened on Thursday 27 September 2007 by Nelson Mandela; R650 million cost; Maponya and Zenprop 42.5% each and Investec 15%; 65,000 square metres on land Maponya bought 28 years earlier, near Chris Hani Baragwanath hospital; originally planned at 45,000 square metres; about 200 stores employing over 1,800 people; Zenprop's count of a record 100,000 visitors on opening day; Maponya's 'I was convinced the people really needed a (shopping) mall, I never stopped'; his resistance to apartheid-government attempts to take the land; failed attempts to develop it, including as a casino (Rodney Weinstein of Zenprop).

sources.title: 'I will die with my boots on' (17 August 2005)
sources.supports: Maponya's plans for the mall on land he had bought 28 years earlier to develop as a modern mall; 50/50 partnership with Zenprop; expected to open in October 2006 at 60,000 square metres and R450 million; 'We will not compromise on quality. It will look like any other modern mall anywhere else'; Soweto's five million people and no mall, residents travelling to town to shop; hope of banishing the belief that black shoppers preferred to spend elsewhere; apartheid restrictions, 'temporary sojourners in the cities'; 'This excites me more than anything else I have done'.

sources.title: Retail Renegade: Richard Maponya (2007)
sources.supports: The mall's site on Old Potchefstroom Road opposite a barber's wooden shack; a $70 million, 65,000 square metre mall opening later that month; Soweto's roughly five million people having to travel to Johannesburg to shop; his early tailoring business closed by the authorities, then a dairy with bicycle delivery, general stores, a butcher, filling stations and GM and BMW dealerships; licensing obstacles under apartheid.

sources.title: Richard John Pelwana Maponya: Order of Ikhamanga citation (archived)
sources.publisher: The Presidency of the Republic of South Africa, via the Internet Archive
sources.supports: Denied a licence for Soweto's first retail clothing store in the 1950s but given a licence to sell foodstuffs; the Dube Hygienic Dairy and bicycle delivery; butchery, grocery stores, restaurant, filling station, GM and BMW dealerships; the long-held dream of building Maponya Mall, 65,000 square metres.

sources.title: How Maponya Mall, the 'heartbeat' of Soweto's economy, was rescued by the community (18 July 2021)
sources.supports: Maponya Mall in Pimville, 65,000 square metres, opened in 2007 at a cost of R650 million; Maponya died in January 2020; during the July 2021 unrest about a dozen malls and shops in Soweto were destroyed while Pimville residents formed a human chain around Maponya Mall's gates, and it was the only large mall in Soweto to survive.

sources.title: Ntate Richard Maponya, the grandfather of black business in SA, dies aged 99 (6 January 2020)
sources.supports: Maponya's death on 6 January 2020 (see research notes on his age).

cross_checks.claim: Maponya Mall opened in Soweto in September 2007 on land Maponya had bought decades earlier.
Maponya had bought the land in the late 1970s (28 years before 2005 or 2007) intending to build a mall.
Under apartheid Maponya was refused a clothing licence and built food, dairy, retail and motor businesses instead.
Zenprop was Maponya's development partner and the mall covered about 65,000 square metres.
Soweto had millions of residents and no mall, so people travelled into town to shop.

research_notes: Cost disagrees: the Mail & Guardian (2005) gave a planned R450 million; Fin24 (opening day, 2007) and Daily Maverick (2021) give R650 million; Time (2007) gives $70 million. The story gives Fin24's R650 million and names Fin24. Size: 60,000 square metres planned (M&G 2005), originally 45,000 (Zenprop's Weinstein, 2007), 65,000 as built (Fin24, Time, Daily Maverick, Presidency). Ownership: 50/50 with Zenprop in 2005 (M&G); 42.5% each with Investec 15% at opening (Fin24); Weinstein said Zenprop and Investec joined 'about 18 months' before opening, which sits awkwardly with M&G's 2005 report of the Zenprop deal, so the story says 'by 2005' for Zenprop only. Year the land was bought: both M&G (2005) and Fin24 (2007) say '28 years ago', which gives 1977 or 1979; Fin24 also says 'nearly 30 years'; the Presidency's 2007 citation says the dream was 26 years old; the story says 'nearly thirty years' and 'late 1970s'. Age: the Presidency gives his birth as 24 December 1926 and Time (2007) called him 80, but TimesLIVE (2020) reported him dying 'aged 99', M&G (2005) said 79 and Fin24 (2007) 82; the story gives no age. The 100,000 opening-day visitors is Zenprop's claim and is attributed to it. The resistance to apartheid attempts to take the land comes from Fin24's report and is attributed to it. TimesLIVE's article body is rendered by script; only its headline and standfirst could be read, so it supports only the date of death, which Daily Maverick also gives. Arc changed from the slate's 'hard-responsibility' to 'breakthrough', since the documented episode is the opening after decades of obstruction; funding changed from 'bootstrapped' to 'mixed' because the mall was built with a property developer (Zenprop) and a bank (Investec) as equity partners. The Presidency citation is cited from an Internet Archive copy because the live page has moved. Tagore wrote Sadhana in English; the passage describes those who hold on to life and work in joy and is applied by analogy.
